title: malloc & free
learningGoals: allocate an array whose size is chosen at run time with `malloc(n * sizeof(int))`
use the memory like a normal array
release it with `free` and then set the pointer to `NULL`

youtube.title: malloc and free: Borrow Memory, Return It | C EP 66
youtube.description: How many students are in the class? You only find out when the program runs. With malloc you ask for exactly that much memory, use it like an array, and give it back with free. We draw every byte, then watch a program leak memory until it runs dry. 0:00 The shamiana hire shop · 0:20 Title · 0:25 Asking for bytes · 1:25 Check, use, free · 2:15 Code, line by line · 4:05 Running it · 4:30 Pun · 4:35 The four-step habit · 5:05 Bug of the Day: forgetting free · 6:15 Challenge · 6:40 Next episode

chapters.label: Bug of the Day: forgetting free

thumbnail.visual: big text "BORROW. RETURN."; a mint heap with a row of crates labelled `marks[0..2]`, a black arrow from `marks`; a tomato "free()" stamp; Xecxec handing back a key; mint background, tomato text block

scenes.onScreen: A Goan wedding shamiana hire shop: "How many chairs?" sign; Xecxec writes "3"; three chairs are carried out; later returned
scenes.animation: Chairs carried out one by one; ledger tick; chairs returned; till-bell
scenes.narration: When your family plans a wedding in Goa, you go to the hire shop for chairs. The shopkeeper asks: how many? You say three hundred. He gives you exactly three hundred, and writes it in his ledger. After the wedding, you return them all. malloc is the hire shop. free is returning the chairs.

scenes.onScreen: Stack: `n` = 3, `marks` (pointer). Heap: a 12-byte block at 0x5000 split into three 4-byte boxes; label "n * sizeof(int) = 3 * 4 = 12 bytes"
scenes.animation: Formula types out; block drops into the heap; arrow draws from `marks` to the first box
scenes.narration: Last episode, we used malloc for one int. Today, a whole array, with a size we only learn while the program is running. Say the user types 3 students. malloc does not understand "3 ints". It only understands bytes. So we calculate: n times sizeof int. 3 times 4 is 12 bytes. malloc finds 12 free bytes in the heap, say at 0x5000, and returns that address. We store it in a pointer called marks. Now look closely: the heap block is three int boxes in a row, and marks points to the first one. That's exactly what an array looks like from EP 57. So we can write marks square bracket i, just like a normal array.

scenes.onScreen: Same diagram; boxes fill with 60, 70, 80; then `free(marks)` greys the block; then `marks = NULL` turns the arrow into a NULL sign
scenes.animation: Values pop in; grey wash on free with a key-return clink; arrow snaps off into a NULL sign
scenes.narration: Now we fill the boxes: 60, 70, 80. When we're done, we call free of marks. The block goes back to the heap. It's greyed out. But look at marks. It still holds 0x5000! free does not change your pointer. The arrow still points at memory you've returned. That's a trap, and we'll study it in EP 68. So after free, we set marks to NULL. Now the arrow is gone, and nobody can use it by mistake.

scenes.onScreen: `marks.c` (29 lines); tracker: n, marks, i, marks[i]
scenes.animation: Butter highlights; corner heap diagram mirrors scenes 3–4
scenes.narration: Here's the program. [HL 2] Line 2 includes stdlib dot h for malloc and free. [HL 5] Line 5 creates n. [HL 6] Line 6 asks how many students. [HL 7] Line 7 reads n with scanf. scanf returns how many values it read. If it's not 1, or if n is zero or negative, [HL 8] line 8 prints an error, [HL 9] and line 9 returns 1. Never pass a negative size to malloc. [TRACK n=3] [HL 12] Line 12 is the key line: int star marks equals malloc of n times sizeof int. We ask for 12 bytes and get the address of the first. [TRACK marks=0x5000] [HL 13] Line 13: if marks is NULL, malloc failed. [HL 14] Line 14 prints a message, [HL 15] and line 15 returns 1. Always check. [HL 18] Lines 18 to 20 fill the array. For our demo, each student gets 60 plus i times 10. [TRACK marks[0]=60] [TRACK marks[1]=70] [TRACK marks[2]=80] [HL 22] Lines 22 to 24 print each student's marks, numbered from 1. [HL 26] Line 26: free of marks. Chairs returned. [HL 27] Line 27: marks equals NULL. Arrow removed. [TRACK marks=NULL] [HL 28] Line 28: return zero.

scenes.animation: First run prints three students; second prints the error line; tomato flash
scenes.narration: Compile and run. Type 3. Student 1: 60, student 2: 70, student 3: 80. Run it again and type 5, and you get five students. Same program, different amount of memory. That's the power of dynamic memory. Now try minus 5. The program politely refuses.

scenes.onScreen: "malloc and free are best friends. One lends, the other always pays back."
scenes.animation: Card flips; Xecxec shakes his own claw; rimshot
scenes.narration: malloc and free are best friends. One lends, the other always pays back.

scenes.onScreen: Four-step habit: 1 malloc with sizeof, 2 check NULL, 3 use, 4 free and set NULL
scenes.animation: Steps tick one by one in mint
scenes.narration: Every time you use malloc, do these four steps. One: malloc with sizeof, never a guessed number. Two: check for NULL. Three: use the memory. Four: free it, and set the pointer to NULL. Make it a habit, like locking your scooter.

scenes.onScreen: `make_order()` that mallocs 4,000 bytes and never frees, called 1,00,000 times; heap filling with grey abandoned crates
scenes.animation: Crates pile up and nobody points at them; a memory meter climbs to about 400 MB; alarm; fixed version adds `free(order);` and the meter stays flat
scenes.narration: Today's bug: forgetting free. Here, a function make_order mallocs 1000 ints, 4000 bytes, and uses it. But it never calls free. When the function returns, its local pointer order disappears from the stack. The heap block is still there, but nobody has its address any more. Nobody can ever free it. That is a memory leak. Now main calls make_order one lakh times. One lakh times 4000 bytes is about 400 megabytes of lost memory. GCC gives no warning, and the program still prints "Done". But open Task Manager while it runs, and you'll see its memory climb. In a program that runs for days, like a server or a game, leaks eventually eat all the RAM. The fix is one line: free of order, before the function ends. On Linux, a tool called Valgrind can find leaks for you, and it reports them as "definitely lost".

scenes.onScreen: "Allocate n marks, read them, print the average" task card
scenes.narration: Your challenge. Ask the user how many marks they have. malloc exactly that many ints. Read each mark with scanf, add them up, and print the average with two decimal places. Then free the memory. With marks 70, 80 and 95, you should get 81.67. Pause and try.

scenes.onScreen: "Next: EP 67 · calloc & realloc — need a bigger basket"
scenes.animation: A fish basket grows bigger; sign-off
scenes.narration: You can now borrow exactly the memory you need, and return it. But what if you need more space later? Next episode: calloc and realloc. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
`gcc -Wall bug.c` gives **no warning**, and the program prints:

Done

But it leaks 1,00,000 × 4,000 bytes (about 400 MB) while running; Task Manager shows its memory climbing. On Linux, Valgrind reports the leak (shown here for a 10-call version):

==3504== 40,000 bytes in 10 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 1 of 1
==3504==    at 0x4846828: malloc (in /usr/libexec/valgrind/vgpreload_memcheck-amd64-linux.so)
==3504==    by 0x10917E: make_order (leak10.c:5)
==3504==    by 0x1091B2: main (leak10.c:12)
bug.why: when the only pointer to a heap block disappears without `free`, that memory can never be returned.

pun: "malloc and free are best friends. One lends, the other always pays back."
challenge: Ask for `n`, `malloc` `n` ints, read each mark, print the average to 2 decimals, then `free`.

shorts.title: Arrays of any size
shorts.hook: "How many students?" with a blinking cursor: "You don't know yet. That's fine."
shorts.script: A normal array needs its size when you write the code. But what if the user decides? malloc of n times sizeof int asks the heap for exactly that many bytes, and gives you the address. Use it like a normal array. Then free it. Like hiring chairs for a wedding.
shorts.caption: Exactly as much memory as you need.

shorts.title: The 4-step malloc habit
shorts.hook: Four mint ticks stamping one after another.
shorts.script: Four steps, every single time. One: malloc with sizeof. Two: check for NULL. Three: use the memory. Four: free it, and set the pointer to NULL. Why the last part? Because free returns the memory, but your pointer still points there.
shorts.caption: Make it muscle memory.

shorts.title: The silent leak
shorts.hook: Memory meter racing up to 400 MB.
shorts.script: This function mallocs 4000 bytes and forgets to free them. When it returns, the pointer is gone, but the memory is not. Call it one lakh times: about 400 megabytes lost. No warning, and the program still prints Done. One line fixes it: free.
shorts.caption: Silent, but deadly.

shorts.title: Best friends
shorts.hook: Two crates labelled malloc and free high-fiving.
shorts.script: malloc and free are best friends. One lends, the other always pays back.
shorts.caption: Friendship goals.

shorts.title: Quiz: how many bytes?
shorts.script: Quick quiz. n is 25. How many bytes does malloc of n times sizeof int ask for, on a normal PC? Answer: 100, because an int is 4 bytes. Now the challenge: read n marks into malloc memory and print the average. Comment your code.
shorts.caption: Did you say 100?
